headline: Massachusetts expands ADU aid with $15 million statewide commitment
dek: A new $5 million pilot will help affordable-housing developers build income-restricted accessory dwelling units as the state adds support for homeowners moving projects toward construction.
body: Massachusetts is adding $5 million to its effort to build accessory dwelling units, bringing the Healey administration’s total commitment to ADU development to $15 million. Governor Maura Healey announced the expansion on Oct. 15 in Lexington, saying the new investment is intended to make small, independent homes easier to finance and build across the state. The announcement comes as Massachusetts tries to add housing within existing neighborhoods rather than relying only on large new developments. The [state’s announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-5-million-to-make-it-easier-and-more-affordable-to-build-adus) says more than 2,000 ADUs have already been approved under the administration’s housing initiatives.

The new money has two distinct parts. The Massachusetts Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities says $10 million will support homeowners with costs and barriers identified through the program’s initial feasibility work. A separate $5 million Community ADU Pilot Program will provide financial assistance to qualified affordable-housing developers who already control property where income-restricted ADUs could be built. The state expects that developer pilot to support construction of 20 to 30 affordable units. The [Massachusetts Housing Partnership](https://www.mhp.net/one-mortgage/adu-incentive-program) will administer the ADU initiative in collaboration with HLC.

That distinction matters for residents. An ADU, sometimes called an in-law apartment, is a self-contained home with its own kitchen, bathroom and entrance on the same property as a primary residence. It can be attached to the main house, created inside it or built as a separate structure. A homeowner may be thinking about an aging parent, an adult child or a rental unit, while a nonprofit or other affordable-housing developer may be trying to create a unit with rent restrictions. The new funding is designed to address those different paths rather than treat every project as a conventional apartment development.

The program’s first phase focused on whether a project could work before an owner committed to construction. MHP’s program page says participating feasibility studies can examine site conditions, zoning and permitting, utility needs, preliminary design questions and high-level costs. The studies do not provide architectural or engineering plans and do not guarantee a permit, financing or construction. That limitation is important: the state’s announcement counts approvals, not completed homes, and the new assistance is meant to help projects move through obstacles that can stop them after the planning stage.

Massachusetts reported 2,084 approved ADUs statewide through the first half of 2026, including 854 approvals during those six months. The housing office said in August that 70% of Massachusetts communities had approved at least one ADU since the beginning of 2025. Lowell, Somerville, Plymouth, Lawrence and Revere were among the communities with the most approvals outside Boston. Those figures describe local approvals, not a guarantee that every approved unit has been financed or built, but they show the scale of the policy change after the state made ADUs easier to pursue.

The announcement also points to a local example. In Lexington, the nonprofit Lexington Housing Assistance Board is moving forward with four income-restricted ADUs, according to the state. The projects illustrate the potential statewide impact of the developer pilot: modest additions on existing properties can create affordable homes without waiting for a large parcel to be assembled. They also show why the program’s focus on site control and construction barriers is different from a general zoning change.

State officials have framed the effort as both a housing-supply program and a way to help people remain connected to their communities. Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll cited young adults who want to stay near where they grew up, older residents who want to remain in their homes and people with disabilities who may be able to live more independently with support nearby. Those are policy goals, not a promise that every ADU will serve each use; the actual household and rent rules will depend on the property, local requirements and the funding track involved.

Independent reporting by [WBZ NewsRadio](https://wheb.iheart.com/featured/lend-a-helping-can/content/massachusetts-allots-15-million-for-accessory-dwelling-unit-construction/) confirmed that the second phase was announced at the Lexington event and described the $10 million homeowner assistance and $5 million developer support. The new announcement does not yet provide a statewide list of awards, a construction start date or a final unit count for the homeowner track. Those details will determine how much of the money reaches projects that are currently stalled by design, utility, permitting or financing costs.

For now, Massachusetts homeowners and developers have a program structure to follow, but not a guarantee of funding. MHP’s public materials direct property owners to compare approved feasibility-study providers and consult local building or planning departments about project rules. The state’s next test will be whether the added assistance converts the more than 2,000 approvals into completed, occupied homes—and whether the developer pilot produces the 20 to 30 income-restricted ADUs officials expect.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Massachusetts expands ADU aid with $15 million commitment
seoDescription: Massachusetts added $5 million for accessory dwelling units, including support for homeowners and a pilot for income-restricted ADUs.
